title: Journalism and Media
description: Ten standalone texts about the people and work behind the news: a small-town newspaper, a fact-checker, an editor's column on corrections, a community radio station, podcasts, calm and critical news reading, a photographer, a student paper, a newspaper baron and a sports reporter.

lessons.title: A Day at the Valley Courier
lessons.summary: The editor of a small weekly newspaper plans, checks and finishes the week's paper in one long Tuesday.
lessons.text:
The Valley Courier is a weekly newspaper in a town of about 6,000 people. Its entire workforce fits in one room: an editor, two reporters, a photographer and a woman who handles advertising and subscriptions. The editor, Ruth Ellison, has run the paper for 19 years, and what follows is an ordinary Tuesday, the day before the paper goes to print.

Ruth arrives at seven, switches on the overhead lights and fills her coffee mug, a white mug with the paper's name printed on its side. Before she opens a single email, she looks at the week's list of stories, with the length of each one and the name of the person writing it.

This week the list has six stories. The town treasurer will present the annual budget at a council meeting tonight. A new pharmacy is opening on Main Street, and the mayor will cut a red ribbon at noon. The Protestant church on Oak Street is holding its autumn food drive. The high school football team has won three games in a row. And a family in the suburbs north of town has asked the paper to write about their grandmother, who turns 100 this week.

At nine, Ruth sends one reporter to the ribbon cutting at the pharmacy and the other to see the treasurer, to read the budget before the meeting. "Reading it in advance is the only way to ask good questions tonight," she tells him. A budget is rarely exciting, she admits, but a good treasurer explains where the town's money goes, and readers deserve to know.

Much of the work, in fact, is checking. The pharmacy owner says the store will create twelve jobs, so the reporter asks how many will be full time. The coach gives a score, and the photographer, who was at the game, confirms it.

Overhead costs are a constant worry. Paper and printing are expensive, and their price rises every year. Many families have moved to the suburbs of the nearby city, and some of them no longer read local news. Still, the Courier has about 2,400 subscribers. When a subscriber calls to change an address, Ruth often takes the new zip code herself, because a paper that cannot reach its readers is not much of a paper. More and more of those zip codes belong to the suburbs.

By evening, the pages are nearly full. The story about the pharmacy has a photo of the mayor cutting the ribbon with giant scissors. The food drive at the Protestant church and the grandmother's birthday are staples of small-town news, the kind of stories that national papers ignore and local readers love. Sports scores are another staple. At ten, Ruth reads every page one last time, puts a staple through a printed copy for her files and washes her mug.

Questions:
How big is the Courier's workforce?
The workforce is five people: an editor, two reporters, a photographer and a woman who handles advertising.
Why does Ruth send a reporter to the treasurer before the meeting?
Reading the budget in advance is the only way to ask good questions at the meeting.
Why do overhead costs worry Ruth?
Paper and printing are expensive, and their price rises every year.
Where have many families moved?
Many families have moved to the suburbs of the nearby city.
What are some staples of small-town news?
The food drive, the grandmother's birthday and sports scores are staples of small-town news.

lessons.title: How a Fact-Checker Works
lessons.summary: A fact-checker at a science magazine explains, step by step, how he tests every claim in an article before it is printed.
lessons.text:
Daniel Brooks works as a fact-checker for a monthly science magazine. Before any article goes to print, he reads it line by line and checks every claim that can be checked: names, dates, numbers, quotes and scientific statements. It is quiet, careful work, and most readers never know that it happens.

First, he prints the article and marks every claim with a pencil. A long feature of 3,000 words may contain 150 of them. Then he treats each claim as a hypothesis rather than a fact. A hypothesis is an idea that may be true but still has to be tested. "The writer believes this sentence is true," Daniel explains. "My job is to treat it as a hypothesis and find out whether the evidence agrees."

The second step is to find the original source. Many claims on the internet are derivative: one website copies a number from another, which copied it from a third, and each copy changes it a little. A derivative report is never good enough for Daniel. He follows the chain back until he reaches the study, the official report or the person who first said it.

The third step is documentation. When a writer quotes a scientist, Daniel asks for the recording or the notes. When a company describes a product, he asks for its technical specifications. Last month, an article said that a new electric bus could travel 600 miles on a single charge, a number that supposedly came from the company itself. The company's own specifications, however, gave a range of 300 miles in good weather. The writer had taken the larger number from a derivative news story, and without documentation it would have gone straight into print.

A single stat can cause a great deal of trouble. In the same issue, an article on farming said that one mutation had made a new kind of tomato twice as sweet as older kinds. The study did describe such a mutation, but it found that the mutation made the fruit about 10 percent sweeter. Daniel changed the stat, and the writer thanked him.

Some claims sound absurd and turn out to be true; others sound reasonable and turn out to be false. A reader once wrote to say that it was absurd to claim that a certain tree could live for 5,000 years. Daniel checked, and the claim was correct. His rule is to neither believe nor dismiss anything until he has seen the evidence.

Many publications have cut their fact-checking staff to save money, and some people ask whether the job is still viable. But he believes that careful checking is the only viable way for a publication to keep its readers' trust, because trust, once lost, is very hard to win back.

Questions:
What does Daniel do first with an article?
He prints it and marks every claim with a pencil.
What is a hypothesis?
A hypothesis is an idea that may be true but still has to be tested.
Why is a derivative report not good enough for Daniel?
Each copy may change the original a little, so he follows the chain back to the first source.
What did the bus company's specifications show?
They showed a range of 300 miles in good weather, not the 600 miles the bus could supposedly travel.
What did the study about the tomato mutation really find?
It found that the mutation made the fruit about 10 percent sweeter, not twice as sweet.

lessons.title: From the Editor: Why We Print Corrections
lessons.summary: In a weekly column, a newspaper editor explains how the paper corrects its mistakes and why corrections matter.
lessons.text:
Every week, on page 2 of this newspaper, there is a small box with the heading "Corrections." This week I would like to explain why it is there, and why I believe it matters.

Last month we printed that the public library closes at six in the evening, when in fact it closes at eight. A reader called the next morning. She was annoyed, and she had every right to be annoyed: she had planned her week around our mistake.

Mistakes manifest themselves in many ways. Most are small: a name spelled wrong, a wrong date, a photo with the wrong caption. Some are more serious. A few years ago, one of our headlines described a group of teenagers in a way that repeated an old stereotype about the part of town they came from. Nobody on our staff intended any harm, but a stereotype does harm whether or not anyone intends it. Prejudice often enters writing quietly, through a word chosen in a hurry, and it may only manifest itself when a reader points it out. We printed a correction and an apology, and we changed the way we write about young people.

That case also taught us about juvenile court. When a young person appears in juvenile court, the law in our state protects his or her name, and we abide by that law without exception. We also abide by a rule of our own: a correction must be as easy to find as the mistake.

In accord with our policy, any reader may report an error by phone, by email or in person. An editor checks the complaint against the reporter's notes and recordings. If the paper was wrong, the correction appears in the next issue, both in the box on page 2 and online, beside the original article. This is in accord with the practice of most serious newspapers.

Some people argue that printing corrections makes a newspaper look weak. I believe the opposite is true. A newspaper that never prints corrections is not a newspaper that never makes mistakes; it is a newspaper that hides them.

Compassion matters as well. Behind most errors there is a tired reporter working against a deadline, and behind most complaints there is a person who was hurt or inconvenienced. I try to treat both with compassion. The reporter needs to learn, not to be shamed in public, and the reader needs to be heard.

So, to the reader who missed the library's evening hours: I beg your pardon. To everyone whose name or words we have gotten wrong, or whom we have described with prejudice: we beg your pardon too, and we are listening.

Questions:
Why was the reader annoyed?
The paper printed the wrong closing time for the library, and she had planned her week around the mistake.
What did the old headline repeat?
It repeated an old stereotype about the part of town some teenagers came from.
What rule does the paper abide by when a young person appears in juvenile court?
It does not print the young person's name, because the state law protects it.
What happens, in accord with the paper's policy, when a reader reports an error?
An editor checks the complaint, and if the paper was wrong, a correction appears in the next issue and online.
Why does the editor treat reporters and readers with compassion?
Reporters often make errors because they are tired, and readers who complain have often been hurt.

lessons.title: The Station Above the Hardware Store
lessons.summary: A small community radio station explains how it works, and how it stayed on the air during a dangerous storm.
lessons.text:
Millbrook Community Radio broadcasts from two small rooms above a hardware store. It is a noncommercial station, which means that it plays no advertisements. Its money comes from listeners' donations, a small grant from the state and a fundraising concert every summer. Because it is noncommercial, the station does not need to attract the largest possible audience. It can play local bands, read the school lunch menus and broadcast town meetings from beginning to end.

The station manager, Grace Lin, is its only paid employee. About forty volunteers do everything else. On a typical Saturday morning, a retired teacher hosts a show about local history, a jazz trio plays live in the tiny studio, and a children's theater group comes in to perform a puppet show. "People laugh when I tell them we have puppets on the radio," Grace says. "But the children at home can't see the puppets, so they imagine them, and that is half the fun." The trio, three friends who have played together since high school, often stays to play music for the puppet show.

Grace is proudest, however, of the station's emergency plan. A small station, she explains, can do something that a large one often cannot: it can talk about one particular road, one particular school or one particular bridge. For that reason, the station keeps a written plan, a backup generator and a list of volunteers who can come in at any hour.

The plan was tested last spring. Late one evening, amid heavy rain, the weather service issued a tornado warning for the county. Grace was at home when her phone began to ping with alerts. It pinged again and again as the warning spread to nearby towns. She took her umbrella, which the wind turned inside out within seconds, and drove to the station with a phone charger and a bag of sandwiches, because she expected a long night.

For six hours, she and two volunteers stayed on the air. Amid the noise of the storm, they read updates from the weather service, listed the shelters that were open and took calls from listeners. Many homes lost power, and many phones died because their owners had no way to use a charger. Battery radios, however, still worked.

One caller, a farmer, described seeing the tornado pass about a mile from her house. "It was terrifying," she said, "but hearing a voice I know made it less terrifying." The tornado damaged several barns but injured no one.

The next week, donations to the station doubled. Grace used part of the money to buy a second generator and a box of spare umbrellas for the volunteers.

Questions:
What does it mean that the station is noncommercial?
It means that the station plays no advertisements.
Who plays music during the puppet show?
A jazz trio, three friends who have played together since high school, plays music for the puppet show.
What happened amid the heavy rain last spring?
The weather service issued a tornado warning for the county.
Why did Grace bring a phone charger to the station?
She expected a long night on the air.
Why did the farmer say the storm was less terrifying?
Hearing a voice she knew on the radio made it less terrifying.

lessons.title: The Rise of Podcasts
lessons.summary: A short report explains how podcasts grew from a hobby into an industry, and weighs what people praise and fear about them.
lessons.text:
Twenty years ago, a podcast was usually a hobby. Two friends, often a pair of college roommates, would place a microphone on the kitchen table, talk for an hour and upload the recording for a few hundred listeners. Today, the number of podcasts has grown dramatically. There are millions of shows, some podcasts are heard internationally by tens of millions of people, and large media companies pay huge sums for the most popular ones.

Part of the reason is technical: smartphones made it easy to listen while driving or cooking, and cheap equipment made it easy to record. But part of the reason is older than any phone. Before television, families sat around the radio to hear dramas, comedies and news. Many observers describe podcasts as a revival of that tradition, a revival of the human voice telling a story to a listener who is doing something else with their hands.

One of the most popular kinds of podcast is the true crime thriller, a series that follows a real investigation over many episodes. Like a thriller novel, it ends each episode with a question. Perhaps more surprising is the success of shows about a single narrow subject. There are podcasts that specialize in the history of one city, in old maps, in beekeeping or in a single novel. Because a podcast costs little to produce, a show can specialize in a topic that a radio station could never afford to cover.

Music is a different story. If a podcast plays a popular song, it usually has to pay royalties to the people who own it, and those royalties can be expensive. For that reason, many podcasts use original music, or no music at all. Questions about royalties are a regular subject at podcasting seminars.

At a university seminar last year, a group of journalists discussed what podcasts mean for the news. One speaker argued that podcasts fuse journalism with entertainment, and that this mix helps serious reporting reach people who would never read a long article. Another speaker worried that the same mix can blur the line between facts and opinions. A popular host can sound like a trusted friend, and listeners may forget to ask whether the host has checked his or her claims.

Both views contain some truth, and the debate is now taking place internationally. A podcast can fuse careful reporting with good storytelling, or it can fuse rumors with confident talk. The format itself is neither good nor bad. As with any source of news, what matters is how the work is done.

And the two roommates at the kitchen table? Many are still recording, for an audience that has grown dramatically, in the same relaxed way.

Questions:
What was a podcast like twenty years ago?
It was usually a hobby, often two roommates talking at a kitchen table.
Why do many observers call podcasts a revival?
Podcasts bring back the old tradition of families listening to stories on the radio.
Why can a podcast specialize in a narrow topic?
A podcast costs little to produce, so it does not need a large audience.
Why do many podcasts avoid popular songs?
They would have to pay royalties to the people who own the songs.
What did the two speakers at the seminar disagree about?
One said that mixing journalism with entertainment helps reporting reach people, and the other worried that it blurs facts and opinions.

lessons.title: How to Read the News Calmly
lessons.summary: A reflective essay offers practical ways to follow the news without being overwhelmed by it.
lessons.text:
We all know the feeling. We pick up the phone to check the weather, and an hour later we are still reading bad news from places we will never visit. We feel informed, but also tired and anxious. The news, which should help us understand the world, has consumed our evening.

This essay is not an argument against the news, which a free society needs. It is an argument for reading it in a calmer and more critical way, so that the news informs us without leaving us consumed by worry.

First, notice how the news reaches us. On a phone, every alert is a small stimulus, a signal that asks the brain to pay attention now. One stimulus does no harm. A hundred of them in a day can keep the mind in a state of constant alarm. It helps to turn off most alerts and to read the news at one or two fixed times a day. Outside those times, the phone becomes less of a distraction, and the evening belongs to you again. A distraction you control is no longer a distraction.

Second, read slowly. Headlines are written to make us blink and click, so read past them. A headline can change in the blink of an eye; the facts usually do not. What is the thrust of the article? The thrust of a story is its main point, and it is often more careful and more modest than the headline suggests. Read the whole piece before deciding what you think.

Third, pay attention to rhetoric. Rhetoric is the art of persuading people, and every good speech uses it. But strong rhetoric can hide weak evidence. When a text uses many emotional words, ask a simple question: what exactly happened, and how does the writer know? Rhetoric from any side of a debate deserves the same question.

Fourth, read widely. A single source, used in conjunction with nothing else, gives a narrow view. Used in conjunction with two or three other sources, including some you tend to disagree with, it gives a fuller picture.

Finally, there is a more philosophical point. Some stories haunt us because we can do nothing about them. It is natural to care, but caring is not the same as reading every update. One philosophical approach, much older than the internet, is to separate what we can change from what we cannot. Read about distant events, then turn to local ones, where you can help.

The news will not be our salvation, and it will not be our ruin; salvation is too large a word for it. It is a tool, and it works best when we use it, not when it uses us. Read the news, then close the page, and do not let it haunt your evening.

Questions:
Why can phone alerts make us anxious?
Each alert is a stimulus, and a hundred of them in a day keep the mind in a state of alarm.
What is the thrust of an article?
It is its main point, which is often more careful than the headline.
What question should readers ask when a text uses strong rhetoric?
They should ask what exactly happened and how the writer knows.
Why should a source be read in conjunction with others?
A single source gives a narrow view, and several sources give a fuller picture.
What philosophical approach does the writer suggest?
The writer suggests separating what we can change from what we cannot.

lessons.title: The Photographer Who Waits
lessons.summary: A profile of a newspaper photographer who spent forty years recording rural life, and of his patient way of working.
lessons.text:
Tom Haskell is 61, tall and completely bald, and he is almost always wearing the same green jacket. For forty years he worked as a photographer for a regional newspaper, and in that time he photographed farmers, fishermen, firefighters, school teachers and two state governors. His pictures have won awards, but when you ask him about his work, he talks less about cameras than about patience.

"Most people think a news photographer has to be fast," he says. "Sometimes, yes. But the best pictures usually come from waiting."

Tom's most famous series began during a drought that lasted three summers. The rivers dropped, the fields turned brown and farmers sold their animals because they could not feed them. Tom spent weeks with one family that had kept cattle for four generations. He photographed the father and his teenage son moving the herd to the last field with water. He photographed the empty barn after the herd was sold. The drought series appeared on the front page, and readers in the cities wrote letters saying that, for the first time, they understood what a drought meant for a family.

Tom also loved the wild places at the edge of the region. He once spent a week in the wilderness to the north, following a team of scientists who were counting birds. The terrain was difficult: steep hills, thick forest and, in the valleys, wide marsh where every step sank into cold mud. He kept his camera dry by tucking it inside his jacket, and he tucked his spare batteries into his shirt pocket so the cold would not drain them. The descent at the end of the trip, down a narrow path in the rain, took a whole day. "The descent was harder than the climb," he remembers. "But the light over the marsh that last morning was worth every hour."

His method has three rules. First, he arrives early, before the people he is photographing are busy, so they can get used to him. Second, he asks permission and explains where the picture will appear. Third, he never stages a picture; he does not tell people where to stand or what to do. "If I arrange the scene, it is no longer news," he says. "It is theater."

Not everyone agrees with that strict view. Some younger photographers argue that a portrait, unlike a news photo, may be arranged as long as the caption says so. Tom respects the argument, but for his own work he keeps his rule.

Today Tom teaches a photography class at the local college. He tells his students what he learned in the wilderness and in the drought: learn the terrain, tuck your camera in when it rains and wait.

Questions:
How does Tom Haskell look?
He is tall and completely bald, and he usually wears a green jacket.
What happened to the herd during the drought?
The family moved the herd to the last field with water, and later the herd was sold.
What was the terrain like in the wilderness?
There were steep hills, thick forest and wide marsh in the valleys.
How did Tom keep his camera dry?
He tucked it inside his jacket.
Why does Tom never stage a picture?
He believes that a staged picture is no longer news.

lessons.title: The Griffin
lessons.summary: A sixteen-year-old student edits her school newspaper and learns how to report a story fairly with help from a teacher.
lessons.text:
The student newspaper at Lincoln High School is called The Griffin, after the school's mascot. A griffin is a creature from old stories, with the body of a lion and the head and wings of an eagle, and a large painted griffin looks down from the wall of the school gym. The paper comes out once a month, and this year its editor is Nora Patel, who is sixteen.

Being sixteen and an editor is not easy. Nora has eight reporters, all of them her friends or classmates, and she has to tell them when a story is not good enough. She also has to meet a deadline every month, while doing her own homework.

The paper's faculty coordinator is Mr. Alvarez, who teaches English. As coordinator, he does not write or choose the stories. His role is to give advice, to teach the reporters basic rules and to make sure the paper is printed on time. "It's your paper," he tells the students every September. "I'm only the coordinator."

This month, Nora has two main stories. The first is about the town's peach festival, which takes place every August and raises money for the school's sports teams. A reporter has interviewed farmers who sell peaches, a baker who makes peach pies and the students who sell cold juice beside the peach stands.

The second story is more difficult. For thirty years, a retired policeman named Frank Lowell has helped children cross the busy street in front of the school. The town council has decided to replace him with a traffic light, and many students are upset. Nora has written a strong article that praises Mr. Lowell and criticizes the council.

She shows the draft to Mr. Alvarez. He reads it slowly. "Hm," he says. "This is a good start. But who on the council did you talk to?"

"Nobody," Nora admits. "Everyone already knows they're wrong."

"Hm. Then you're writing an opinion, not a report," he says. "Call the council first and ask why they decided this. That'll make the story fair, and it'll make it stronger, too."

Nora calls a council member the next day. She learns that the street has become much busier and that the council plans to give the retired policeman a new job at the school's main gate. Nora rewrites the article, using quotes from both the council member and the old policeman.

When the paper comes out, Mr. Lowell asks for ten copies. "That'll be enough for my grandchildren," he says, smiling. Nora puts the front page of The Griffin on her bedroom wall.

Questions:
What is a griffin?
It is a creature from old stories, with the body of a lion and the head and wings of an eagle.
What does Mr. Alvarez do as the paper's coordinator?
He gives advice, teaches basic rules and makes sure the paper is printed on time.
What does the peach festival raise money for?
It raises money for the school's sports teams.
What was missing from Nora's first draft?
She had not talked to anyone on the town council.
What will happen to the retired policeman?
The council plans to give him a new job at the school's main gate.

lessons.title: The Baron of Front Street
lessons.summary: A local history column tells how a wealthy newspaper owner built and lost a town's first daily paper, and compares newspaper ownership then and now.
lessons.text:
If you walk down Front Street today, you will pass a seven-story brick building with tall windows and stone eagles above the door. Most people know it as an office building. Few remember that it was built in 1912 as the home of the Daily Herald, and that it belonged to a man whom his rivals called "the baron."

Charles Whitmore was a newspaper baron in the full sense of the term. A baron was once a nobleman who held land from a king; in the age of newspapers, the word came to mean a businessman who owned many papers and used them to gain influence. By 1910, Whitmore owned eleven papers in four states. He chose our town for his new headquarters because it was close to the railroad and to the sea.

The Herald building was the most elegant in the region. When it was finished, it dwarfed every other building in town; the bank across the street, then considered large, looked like a toy beside it. Whitmore lived in a penthouse on the top floor, with a roof garden and a view of the sea. Whitmore's household had a staff of four, including a cook and a maid. Years later, the maid, a young woman named Helen Ward, described her work there in a letter that the town library still keeps. She wrote that Whitmore read every page of the paper before it was printed, often late at night, while she brought him coffee.

In summer, Whitmore sailed his yacht from the mainland to a small island he owned, about ten miles off the coast. Visitors to the island remembered elegant dinners on the yacht, where politicians and business leaders discussed the news of the day. Critics said that this was exactly the problem: a single rich man could decide what thousands of readers on the mainland would learn.

The baron's fortune did not last. In the hard years after 1929, advertising fell sharply, and Whitmore borrowed heavily to keep his papers going. When he could not repay, his main lender went to court. In 1932 a court decree ordered the Herald sold, and a second decree, a year later, transferred the building to the lender. Whitmore died soon after. In accordance with his wishes, his burial took place on his island, and a small boat carried his family to the burial at sunrise.

Today, the elegant old building is dwarfed by the modern towers near the highway, and the town's newspaper is owned by a group of local investors. Some historians argue that the baron, for all his faults, gave the town a serious daily paper. Others point out that a newspaper is healthier when no one person controls it. Both views are worth remembering when you walk down Front Street.

Questions:
What did the word baron come to mean in the age of newspapers?
It came to mean a businessman who owned many papers and used them to gain influence.
Where did Whitmore live?
He lived in a penthouse on the top floor of the Herald building.
What did the maid write about Whitmore?
She wrote that he read every page of the paper before it was printed.
What did the court decree of 1932 order?
It ordered the Herald sold.
Where did Whitmore's burial take place?
His burial took place on his island.

lessons.title: On the Sports Desk
lessons.summary: A regional sports reporter covers a busy weekend and explains how she writes a fair and lively game report on deadline.
lessons.text:
Maya Torres has covered sports for a regional newspaper for nine years. People sometimes assume that her job is mostly watching games, but, as she explains, the watching is the easy part. The hard part is turning 90 minutes of action into 600 clear words in less than an hour.

Last weekend was typical. On Saturday morning, she covered a golf tournament at the country club. She stood near the first tee, where each player hits the opening shot, and wrote down the names, the times and anything unusual. A golfer who arrives at the tee late or nervous may be the story of the day. By noon, she had moved on to the cycling race through the hills west of town.

The race had one clear favorite: a 20-year-old cyclist from a nearby village who hoped to surpass the course record. The young cyclist was ambitious, and she had trained on the course all summer. She did surpass the record, by eleven seconds, and Maya interviewed her at the finish line while she was still out of breath. "I'm just relieved," the cyclist said. "I didn't want to disappoint everyone who came to watch."

On Saturday evening came the main event: a game of the city's professional soccer team. Before the game, the crowd stood for the national anthem, and Maya stood with them at the back of the press box. When the anthem ended, she opened her laptop. The night was cold, and by the second half her fingers were so stiff that she typed with gloves on.

Maya always writes during the game, not after it. By halftime, she had a draft of the first half, with space for the ending. The home team won 2 to 1, and the player of the night was a young midfielder who controlled the center of the field. His passing was superb, and his second goal, from twenty yards, was the best of the season. There was also a costly mistake: in the final minutes, the visiting goalkeeper dropped an easy ball, and that costly error decided the game.

Writing about mistakes requires care, so Maya described what happened simply and fairly, without mocking the player. "Everyone makes mistakes," she says. "Mine just don't happen in front of 20,000 people." After the game, she went to the locker rooms for quotes. The midfielder thanked his teammates. The goalkeeper, to his credit, answered every question.

At eleven, her story was finished. She checked the names, the scores and the minute of each goal, then sent it to her editor. Her fingers were still stiff, but she was relieved. On Sunday she would write a longer piece about the ambitious young cyclist and her new record, which may take years to surpass.

Questions:
Where did Maya stand at the golf tournament?
She stood near the first tee, where each player hits the opening shot.
What did the young cyclist do?
She surpassed the course record by eleven seconds.
Why did Maya type with gloves on?
The night was cold, and her fingers were stiff.
Who was the player of the night?
A young midfielder whose passing was superb was the player of the night.
What costly mistake decided the game?
The visiting goalkeeper dropped an easy ball in the final minutes.
